Ryan Clark is a heck of an analyst, but for me, this is some of his finest work. It didn’t happen at ESPN or in talking Xs and Os, but on The Pivot. He got Carl Nassib to open up about the death of his Uncle Bill and how it served as a catalyst for his coming out. Ryan also asked about his first game playing since he came out, when there were “no more secrets” — a game in which he had a sack fumble. I thought this was a really smart, emotionally intelligent question because it gave insight into the burden closeted athletes carry and how freeing this was for him. On a broader level, it also showed how closely our emotions — even subconsciously — are tied to our performance. And it revealed a hilarious story from when the Raiders played the Browns. It made me laugh. It made me cry. That’s what good interviews do. The sincerity with which Ryan, Channing Crowder and Fred Taylor all approached this topic and the respect shown for Carl really came through on this. It’s also not lost on me that a group of men whose voices are so widely respected around the league painted a picture of what acceptance looks like in a locker room. This conversation is very similar to the dynamic I observed in Tampa after Carl came out. Carl didn’t have to hide who he was. He brought his then-partner to outings with teammates. I hope Ryan continues to facilitate these types of vulnerable conversations, which I think are incredibly important, especially among men who quite often don’t have enough spaces to do it in. They’re also incredibly important for those of us who need to hear them so we can better understand the people we care about. Proud to work with you, @Realrclark25. Thank you for being an incredible teammate https://t.co/1GuuImRCyj

Broncos OC and primary play-caller Davis Webb, when asked last month about calling plays with Sean Payton potentially leaning over his shoulder, metaphorically speaking: "I would say just two things about that. No. 1, that was one reason why I wanted to be here -- was with Sean here. I trust him. He trusts me. We think very similar. I know how he wants the game to be played. It's the same offense, for the most part -- just little tweaks here and there, but this is a Sean Payton-coached football team, a Sean Payton offensive philosophy, and we're just gonna grow with our QB and our skill players and our offensive line. ... This is a fun offense to be a part of, and the most attractive thing was leaning on Sean, being in game-plan meetings with him, using his experience. I think that's going to benefit a young play-caller. I'm not dumb. I know this is a lot. However, having him there and having the relationship with the staff members, I love our staff."

Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph says that part of the challenge for his defense after two stellar seasons is "human nature." As he explains, "I told the guys the very first day that we're not chasing what we've done the last two years, but we're chasing the process that got us there. And that's tough for players and coaches alike. The process is tough and it takes a long time to be really good at something, and once the season's over, what you did last year doesn't matter, and that feels like a waste. Starting over is the key, finding ways to get better ... We have to find ways to get better, taking the ball away and those things."

Ryan Clark is a heck of an analyst, but for me, this is some of his finest work. It didn’t happen at ESPN or in talking Xs and Os, but on The Pivot. He got Carl Nassib to open up about the death of his Uncle Bill and how it served as a catalyst for his coming out. Ryan also asked about his first game playing since he came out, when there were “no more secrets” — a game in which he had a sack fumble. I thought this was a really smart, emotionally intelligent question because it gave insight into the burden closeted athletes carry and how freeing this was for him. On a broader level, it also showed how closely our emotions — even subconsciously — are tied to our performance. And it revealed a hilarious story from when the Raiders played the Browns. It made me laugh. It made me cry. That’s what good interviews do. The sincerity with which Ryan, Channing Crowder and Fred Taylor all approached this topic and the respect shown for Carl really came through on this. It’s also not lost on me that a group of men whose voices are so widely respected around the league painted a picture of what acceptance looks like in a locker room. This conversation is very similar to the dynamic I observed in Tampa after Carl came out. Carl didn’t have to hide who he was. He brought his then-partner to outings with teammates. I hope Ryan continues to facilitate these types of vulnerable conversations, which I think are incredibly important, especially among men who quite often don’t have enough spaces to do it in. They’re also incredibly important for those of us who need to hear them so we can better understand the people we care about. Proud to work with you, @Realrclark25.
